blocks.en: Orientation: When the Persecutor Becomes the Patron
blocks.es_reference: Orientación: Cuando el perseguidor se convierte en patrón

blocks.en: For three centuries the church had asked one question above all others: how do we survive Rome? Then almost overnight, between 312 and 313, that question vanished and was replaced by one almost no one had thought to prepare for: how do we survive Rome's friendship?
blocks.es_reference: Por tres siglos la iglesia había hecho una pregunta por encima de todas las demás: ¿cómo sobrevivimos a Roma? Entonces casi de la noche a la mañana, entre 312 y 313, esa pregunta desapareció y fue reemplazada por una para la que casi nadie se había preparado: ¿cómo sobrevivimos a la amistad de Roma?

blocks.en: Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge in October 312 changed everything. The Edict of Milan in 313 granted Christians freedom of worship, restored confiscated property, and ended the era in which Christians could be subjected to periodic and sometimes empire-wide imperial persecution. Within a generation Christianity would be the favored religion of the empire. Bishops who had hidden in caves now sat in conference with the emperor. Buildings that had been illegal now rose as basilicas at imperial expense. The blood of the martyrs had become the seed of an established church.
blocks.es_reference: La victoria de Constantino en el Puente Milvio en octubre del 312 cambió todo. El Edicto de Milán en 313 otorgó a los cristianos la libertad de adorar, restauró la propiedad confiscada, y terminó la era en que los cristianos podían ser sometidos a persecución imperial periódica y a veces imperio-extensa. Dentro de una generación el cristianismo sería la religión favorecida del imperio. Obispos que se habían escondido en cuevas ahora se sentaban en conferencia con el emperador. Edificios que habían sido ilegales ahora se levantaban como basílicas a expensas imperiales. La sangre de los mártires se había convertido en la semilla de una iglesia establecida.

blocks.en: This was the right answer to a three-hundred-year prayer, and a problem the church had never had to solve. Unit 3 is the story of how the church wrestled the new questions through the fourth and early fifth centuries, defined her doctrine of God and Christ in the four great ecumenical councils, and produced — while she was at it — the second great century of preaching in her history.
blocks.es_reference: Esta era la respuesta correcta a una oración de trescientos años, y un problema que la iglesia nunca había tenido que resolver. La Unidad 3 es la historia de cómo la iglesia luchó con las nuevas preguntas a través del cuarto y principios del quinto siglo, definió su doctrina de Dios y de Cristo en los cuatro grandes concilios ecuménicos, y produjo — mientras tanto — el segundo gran siglo de predicación en su historia.

blocks.en: "This is the faith of the universal Church which has been delivered from of old." — Athanasius
blocks.es_reference: «Esta es la fe de la Iglesia universal que ha sido entregada desde antaño». — Atanasio

blocks.en: I. Constantine, Edict of Milan, and the Donatist Problem
blocks.es_reference: I. Constantino, el Edicto de Milán, y el problema donatista

blocks.en: Constantine was a soldier and politician, not a theologian. The night before the Milvian Bridge, according to his biographer Eusebius, he saw a sign in the sky — a cross of light with the words "In this sign conquer." He marked his soldiers' shields with the Christian Chi-Rho, won the battle, and attributed the victory to the Christian God. From that day forward Constantine considered himself a patron of the church, though he was not actually baptized until just before his death in 337.
blocks.es_reference: Constantino era un soldado y político, no un teólogo. La noche antes del Puente Milvio, según su biógrafo Eusebio, vio una señal en el cielo — una cruz de luz con las palabras «Con esta señal vencerás». Marcó los escudos de sus soldados con el Chi-Rho cristiano, ganó la batalla, y atribuyó la victoria al Dios cristiano. Desde ese día Constantino se consideró patrón de la iglesia, aunque no fue realmente bautizado hasta justo antes de su muerte en 337.

blocks.en: His policy was simple: support, protect, unify. He returned confiscated property, gave clergy tax exemptions, commissioned new church buildings, summoned bishops to imperial conferences. He expected the church to be one church, not feuding factions. The first major test came almost immediately, in North Africa, in the Donatist controversy.
blocks.es_reference: Su política era simple: apoyar, proteger, unificar. Devolvió propiedades confiscadas, dio exenciones fiscales al clero, comisionó nuevos edificios eclesiales, convocó obispos a conferencias imperiales. Esperaba que la iglesia fuera una iglesia, no facciones en disputa. La primera prueba mayor vino casi inmediatamente, en África del Norte, en la controversia donatista.

blocks.en: During Diocletian's persecution some North African bishops had handed over the Scriptures to be burned rather than face death. They were called traditores — "those who have handed over." After persecution ended, a man named Caecilian was consecrated bishop of Carthage by another bishop accused of having been a traditor. A rigorist faction refused to accept the consecration. They argued that any sacrament administered by a fallen bishop — baptism, ordination, communion — was invalid. They elected their own bishop, Donatus, and the Donatist church began.
blocks.es_reference: Durante la persecución de Diocleciano algunos obispos norteafricanos habían entregado las Escrituras para ser quemadas en lugar de enfrentar la muerte. Eran llamados traditores — «los que entregaron». Después que la persecución terminó, un hombre llamado Ceciliano fue consagrado obispo de Cartago por otro obispo acusado de haber sido traditor. Una facción rigorista rehusó aceptar la consagración. Argumentaban que cualquier sacramento administrado por un obispo caído — bautismo, ordenación, comunión — era inválido. Eligieron su propio obispo, Donato, y la iglesia donatista comenzó.

blocks.en: The mainstream church, defended most powerfully by Augustine a century later, took a different position: the validity of the sacrament depends on Christ, not on the worthiness of the minister. A baptism is a baptism even when performed by an unworthy bishop, because it is Christ who does the baptizing, not the bishop's hands. This principle — the sacrament is ex opere operato, "from the work performed," rather than dependent on the minister's holiness — would shape Western theology for the next thousand years. The Donatist controversy is a permanent warning against confusing the church's purity with the worthiness of her ministers.
blocks.es_reference: La iglesia principal, defendida con mayor poder por Agustín un siglo después, tomó una posición diferente: la validez del sacramento depende de Cristo, no de la dignidad del ministro. Un bautismo es un bautismo aun cuando es realizado por un obispo indigno, porque es Cristo quien bautiza, no las manos del obispo. Este principio — el sacramento es ex opere operato, «por la obra realizada», en lugar de depender de la santidad del ministro — moldearía la teología occidental por los siguientes mil años. La controversia donatista es una advertencia permanente contra confundir la pureza de la iglesia con la dignidad de sus ministros.

blocks.en: II. The Arian Crisis: Who Is Jesus Christ?
blocks.es_reference: II. La crisis arriana: ¿Quién es Jesucristo?

blocks.en: The Donatist controversy was about the church. The Arian controversy was about Christ Himself, and it was the most serious theological crisis the church had ever faced. The Arian crisis nearly split the empire, occupied four ecumenical councils, and forced the church to put into precise language what it had always confessed: that Jesus Christ is fully and truly God.
blocks.es_reference: La controversia donatista era sobre la iglesia. La controversia arriana era sobre Cristo mismo, y fue la crisis teológica más seria que la iglesia había enfrentado jamás. La crisis arriana casi dividió el imperio, ocupó cuatro concilios ecuménicos, y forzó a la iglesia a poner en lenguaje preciso lo que siempre había confesado: que Jesucristo es plena y verdaderamente Dios.

blocks.en: The trouble began around 318 in Alexandria. A presbyter named Arius was teaching publicly that the Son was not eternal. Arius reasoned: the Father is unbegotten, eternal, without beginning. The Son is begotten of the Father, which means the Son had a beginning. "There was when He was not." The Son is the highest of God's creatures, the first and most exalted of all created beings, but He is still a creature. He is not, properly speaking, God. He is not co-eternal with the Father.
blocks.es_reference: El problema comenzó alrededor del 318 en Alejandría. Un presbítero llamado Arrio estaba enseñando públicamente que el Hijo no era eterno. Arrio razonaba: el Padre es no engendrado, eterno, sin principio. El Hijo es engendrado del Padre, lo que significa que el Hijo tuvo un principio. «Hubo cuando Él no era». El Hijo es la más alta de las criaturas de Dios, el primero y más exaltado de todos los seres creados, pero sigue siendo una criatura. Él no es, propiamente hablando, Dios. Él no es coeterno con el Padre.

blocks.en: Arius's argument had a certain crispness. He was a popular preacher, a clever rhetorician, and he wrote his theology in catchy songs that spread through the docks of Alexandria. By the early 320s the controversy was disrupting the entire eastern church. Constantine was alarmed. He had supported Christianity in part to provide unity for his empire, and now Christians were dividing over a question he could not entirely follow. He decided to call a council. Every bishop in the empire would be invited, fed at imperial expense, and they would settle the question once and for all in the imperial city of Nicaea, in the summer of 325.
blocks.es_reference: El argumento de Arrio tenía una cierta nitidez. Era un predicador popular, un retórico inteligente, y escribía su teología en canciones pegadizas que se extendían por los muelles de Alejandría. Para principios del 320 la controversia estaba interrumpiendo toda la iglesia oriental. Constantino estaba alarmado. Había apoyado el cristianismo en parte para proveer unidad a su imperio, y ahora los cristianos se dividían sobre una pregunta que él no podía seguir enteramente. Decidió convocar un concilio. Cada obispo en el imperio sería invitado, alimentado a expensas imperiales, y resolverían la pregunta de una vez por todas en la ciudad imperial de Nicea, en el verano del 325.

blocks.en: III. Nicaea (325) and the Nicene Creed
blocks.es_reference: III. Nicea (325) y el Credo de Nicea

blocks.en: About 318 bishops attended Nicaea — the number is traditional. Many bore the scars of Diocletian's persecution: missing eyes, severed limbs, ruined hands. They were not theological abstractions. They were men who had bled for the name of Jesus Christ. Now they were being asked to put into a single Greek word what that name meant. The word they chose was homoousios — of the same substance. The Son is not like the Father (homoiousios, with one extra letter). The Son is of the same substance as the Father — fully God, eternally God, equal to the Father in deity.
blocks.es_reference: Alrededor de 318 obispos asistieron a Nicea — el número es tradicional. Muchos llevaban las cicatrices de la persecución de Diocleciano: ojos perdidos, miembros amputados, manos arruinadas. No eran abstracciones teológicas. Eran hombres que habían sangrado por el nombre de Jesucristo. Ahora se les pedía poner en una sola palabra griega lo que ese nombre significaba. La palabra que escogieron fue homoousios — de la misma sustancia. El Hijo no es semejante al Padre (homoiousios, con una letra extra). El Hijo es de la misma sustancia que el Padre — plenamente Dios, eternamente Dios, igual al Padre en deidad.

blocks.en: The original Nicene Creed: "We believe in one God, the Father Almighty… And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father… God of God, Light of Light, true God of true God, begotten not made, of the same substance as the Father…" Almost every clause was aimed at Arius. Begotten not made — against the Arian claim that the Son was created. Of the same substance — the homoousios. True God of true God — reversing Arius's claim that the Son was God only in a derivative sense. The creed concluded with anathemas: "Those who say there was when He was not… the Catholic Church anathematizes." Three hundred and sixteen bishops signed. Two refused and were exiled with Arius. Constantine considered the matter settled. It was not.
blocks.es_reference: El Credo de Nicea original: «Creemos en un solo Dios, Padre Todopoderoso… Y en un solo Señor Jesucristo, Hijo unigénito de Dios, engendrado del Padre… Dios de Dios, Luz de Luz, Dios verdadero de Dios verdadero, engendrado no hecho, de la misma sustancia que el Padre…» Casi cada cláusula apuntaba a Arrio. Engendrado no hecho — contra la afirmación arriana de que el Hijo fue creado. De la misma sustancia — el homoousios. Dios verdadero de Dios verdadero — revirtiendo la afirmación de Arrio de que el Hijo era Dios solo en un sentido derivado. El credo concluyó con anatemas: «A los que dicen que hubo cuando Él no era… la Iglesia Católica anatematiza». Trescientos dieciséis obispos firmaron. Dos rehusaron y fueron exiliados con Arrio. Constantino consideró el asunto resuelto. No lo estaba.

blocks.en: The fifty years after Nicaea were chaos. Different emperors took different sides. Synods met in different cities and issued different creeds. Arian and semi-Arian formulas multiplied. Jerome later said, "The whole world groaned and marveled to find itself Arian." The Nicene confession nearly went under. It survived because of one man.
blocks.es_reference: Los cincuenta años después de Nicea fueron caos. Diferentes emperadores tomaron diferentes lados. Sínodos se reunieron en diferentes ciudades y emitieron diferentes credos. Las fórmulas arrianas y semiarrianas se multiplicaron. Jerónimo después dijo: «El mundo entero gimió y se asombró al descubrirse arriano». La confesión nicena casi se hundió. Sobrevivió a causa de un hombre.

blocks.en: IV. Athanasius Contra Mundum
blocks.es_reference: IV. Atanasio contra el mundo

blocks.en: Athanasius was about thirty years old at Nicaea, a young deacon serving as secretary to his bishop Alexander. Three years later he became bishop of Alexandria himself. For the next forty-five years he defended the Nicene confession against successive Arian and semi-Arian emperors, was exiled five times to four different countries, returned five times, and outlived nearly every one of his enemies. The Latin phrase Athanasius contra mundum — "Athanasius against the world" — captures both his isolation and his stubbornness. When the empire was Arian, Athanasius was Nicene. When his fellow bishops compromised, Athanasius would not.
blocks.es_reference: Atanasio tenía alrededor de treinta años en Nicea, un joven diácono sirviendo como secretario de su obispo Alejandro. Tres años después se convirtió él mismo en obispo de Alejandría. Por los siguientes cuarenta y cinco años defendió la confesión nicena contra sucesivos emperadores arrianos y semiarrianos, fue exiliado cinco veces a cuatro países diferentes, regresó cinco veces, y sobrevivió a casi cada uno de sus enemigos. La frase latina Athanasius contra mundum — «Atanasio contra el mundo» — captura tanto su aislamiento como su tenacidad. Cuando el imperio era arriano, Atanasio era niceno. Cuando sus compañeros obispos comprometían, Atanasio no.

blocks.en: His major works include On the Incarnation, written when he was barely in his twenties — one of the masterpieces of Christian theology, arguing that only a Christ who was fully God could save fully human beings, and only a Christ who was fully man could heal humanity. He wrote Four Discourses Against the Arians, the great anti-Arian polemic. And he gave the church a final gift in his Easter letter of 367: the first known list of the twenty-seven New Testament books we still receive as canonical, in the order we still use. Athanasius did not invent the canon — the church had been recognizing these books for centuries — but his Easter letter formally closed the canon question Marcion had raised two centuries earlier.
blocks.es_reference: Sus obras mayores incluyen De la Encarnación, escrita cuando apenas tenía veintitantos — una de las obras maestras de la teología cristiana, argumentando que solo un Cristo que era plenamente Dios podía salvar plenamente a seres humanos, y solo un Cristo que era plenamente hombre podía sanar la humanidad. Escribió Cuatro Discursos contra los Arrianos, la gran polémica antiarriana. Y le dio a la iglesia un regalo final en su carta pascual del 367: la primera lista conocida de los veintisiete libros del Nuevo Testamento que aún recibimos como canónicos, en el orden que aún usamos. Atanasio no inventó el canon — la iglesia había estado reconociendo estos libros por siglos — pero su carta pascual cerró formalmente la cuestión del canon que Marción había planteado dos siglos antes.

blocks.en: Athanasius did not live to see his vindication. He died in 373. Eight years later, at the Council of Constantinople in 381, the Nicene confession was reaffirmed and expanded, and Arianism was finally crushed within the empire.
blocks.es_reference: Atanasio no vivió para ver su vindicación. Murió en 373. Ocho años después, en el Concilio de Constantinopla en 381, la confesión nicena fue reafirmada y expandida, y el arrianismo fue finalmente aplastado dentro del imperio.

blocks.en: V. The Cappadocians and Constantinople (381)
blocks.es_reference: V. Los Capadocios y Constantinopla (381)

blocks.en: Three friends from the Roman province of Cappadocia (modern central Turkey) finished what Athanasius had begun. They are called the Cappadocian Fathers. Basil the Great (c. 330–379) was bishop of Caesarea, wrote a monastic rule that still governs Eastern Orthodox monasticism, built hospitals and schools at Caesarea that pioneered organized Christian charity, and wrote a treatise On the Holy Spirit defending the Spirit's full deity. Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–389), Basil's lifelong friend, earned the title the Theologian — given by the Eastern church only to him, the apostle John, and Symeon the New Theologian. His Five Theological Orations are masterpieces of patristic preaching. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395) was Basil's younger brother and a more philosophical mind — sometimes called the philosopher of the Cappadocians.
blocks.es_reference: Tres amigos de la provincia romana de Capadocia (la moderna Turquía central) terminaron lo que Atanasio había comenzado. Se llaman los Padres Capadocios. Basilio el Grande (c. 330–379) fue obispo de Cesarea, escribió una regla monástica que aún gobierna el monaquismo ortodoxo oriental, construyó hospitales y escuelas en Cesarea que fueron pioneros en la caridad cristiana organizada, y escribió un tratado Sobre el Espíritu Santo defendiendo la plena deidad del Espíritu. Gregorio de Nacianzo (c. 329–389), amigo de toda la vida de Basilio, se ganó el título de el Teólogo — dado por la iglesia oriental solo a él, al apóstol Juan, y a Simeón el Nuevo Teólogo. Sus Cinco Discursos Teológicos son obras maestras de la predicación patrística. Gregorio de Nisa (c. 335–395) fue el hermano menor de Basilio y una mente más filosófica — a veces llamado el filósofo de los Capadocios.

blocks.en: The Cappadocians gave the church the formula that has held the doctrine of the Trinity steady for sixteen centuries: one ousia (substance) in three hypostases (persons). One God in three Persons. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, equal in essence, distinct in person. The Council of Constantinople in 381 took this formula, expanded the Nicene Creed to confess the full deity of the Spirit, and gave the church the creed she still recites every Lord's Day.
blocks.es_reference: Los Capadocios le dieron a la iglesia la fórmula que ha sostenido firme la doctrina de la Trinidad por dieciséis siglos: una ousia (sustancia) en tres hypostases (personas). Un solo Dios en tres Personas. Padre, Hijo, y Espíritu Santo, iguales en esencia, distintos en persona. El Concilio de Constantinopla en 381 tomó esta fórmula, expandió el Credo de Nicea para confesar la plena deidad del Espíritu, y le dio a la iglesia el credo que aún recita cada Día del Señor.

blocks.en: VI. Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451)
blocks.es_reference: VI. Éfeso (431) y Calcedonia (451)

blocks.en: The Trinity had been settled by 381. The doctrine of Christ's person had not. If the Son is fully God and fully man, how do those two natures relate in the one Person of Jesus? Two more councils answered.
blocks.es_reference: La Trinidad había sido resuelta para 381. La doctrina de la persona de Cristo no. Si el Hijo es plenamente Dios y plenamente hombre, ¿cómo se relacionan esas dos naturalezas en la única Persona de Jesús? Dos concilios más respondieron.

blocks.en: The Council of Ephesus in 431: Nestorius of Constantinople had been preaching that the divine Son and the human Jesus were so distinct that Mary should not be called theotokos (God-bearer). She was the mother of the man Jesus only, Nestorius said. Cyril of Alexandria and the council fiercely disagreed. The one who was born of Mary was the one Person, fully divine and fully human. To split him into two persons was to lose the Christ of the gospel. The council condemned Nestorianism and affirmed Mary as theotokos — not because Mary is divine, but because the One she carried truly was God incarnate.
blocks.es_reference: El Concilio de Éfeso en 431: Nestorio de Constantinopla había estado predicando que el Hijo divino y el Jesús humano eran tan distintos que María no debía ser llamada theotokos (portadora de Dios). Era la madre del hombre Jesús solamente, dijo Nestorio. Cirilo de Alejandría y el concilio estuvieron ferozmente en desacuerdo. Aquel que nació de María era la única Persona, plenamente divino y plenamente humano. Dividirlo en dos personas era perder al Cristo del evangelio. El concilio condenó el nestorianismo y afirmó a María como theotokos — no porque María sea divina, sino porque Aquel a quien llevó era verdaderamente Dios encarnado.

blocks.en: The Council of Chalcedon in 451, perhaps the most important Christological statement the church has ever produced, faced the opposite error: Monophysitism, which taught that Christ had only one nature, the divine swallowing the human. Chalcedon rejected this and gave the church its definitive Christological formula: Jesus Christ is one Person in two natures, fully God and fully man, the two natures united without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. The Chalcedonian Definition has been the standard of orthodox Christology ever since.
blocks.es_reference: El Concilio de Calcedonia en 451, quizás la declaración cristológica más importante que la iglesia ha producido jamás, enfrentó el error opuesto: el monofisismo, que enseñaba que Cristo tenía solo una naturaleza, la divina tragando a la humana. Calcedonia rechazó esto y le dio a la iglesia su fórmula cristológica definitiva: Jesucristo es una Persona en dos naturalezas, plenamente Dios y plenamente hombre, las dos naturalezas unidas sin confusión, sin cambio, sin división, sin separación. La Definición Calcedoniana ha sido el estándar de la cristología ortodoxa desde entonces.

blocks.en: By 451 the church had her doctrine of God (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one in essence, three in person) and her doctrine of Christ (one Person, fully God and fully man, two natures unconfused). The first four ecumenical councils — Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381, Ephesus 431, Chalcedon 451 — together produced the orthodox confession of the catholic faith.
blocks.es_reference: Para 451 la iglesia tenía su doctrina de Dios (Padre, Hijo, y Espíritu Santo, uno en esencia, tres en persona) y su doctrina de Cristo (una Persona, plenamente Dios y plenamente hombre, dos naturalezas no confundidas). Los primeros cuatro concilios ecuménicos — Nicea 325, Constantinopla 381, Éfeso 431, Calcedonia 451 — juntos produjeron la confesión ortodoxa de la fe católica.

blocks.en: VII. The Fourth Century: The Second Great Age of Preaching
blocks.es_reference: VII. El cuarto siglo: La segunda gran era de la predicación

blocks.en: The fourth century is the second of the four great centuries of preaching, and it deserves a close look. Five reasons made it great. First, post-Constantine freedom let preachers speak in the open. Second, classical rhetorical training met biblical content — most fathers had been educated in Greek or Latin rhetoric before conversion. Third, theological controversies forced precision. When you are preaching against Arius, every word matters. Fourth, the cities were full of new converts who needed instruction. Fifth, Constantine's basilicas gave preachers what catacombs never had: large, acoustically generous public spaces with congregations of thousands.
blocks.es_reference: El cuarto siglo es el segundo de los cuatro grandes siglos de la predicación, y merece una mirada cercana. Cinco razones lo hicieron grande. Primera, la libertad post-Constantino dejó que los predicadores hablaran al aire libre. Segunda, el entrenamiento retórico clásico se encontró con el contenido bíblico — la mayoría de los padres habían sido educados en retórica griega o latina antes de la conversión. Tercera, las controversias teológicas forzaron la precisión. Cuando estás predicando contra Arrio, cada palabra importa. Cuarta, las ciudades estaban llenas de nuevos conversos que necesitaban instrucción. Quinta, las basílicas de Constantino dieron a los predicadores lo que las catacumbas nunca tuvieron: espacios públicos grandes y acústicamente generosos con congregaciones de miles.

blocks.en: John Chrysostom (c. 349–407) — "Golden Mouth"
blocks.es_reference: Juan Crisóstomo (c. 349–407) — «Boca de Oro»

blocks.en: If you remember only one fourth-century preacher, remember Chrysostom. The Greek nickname Chrysostomos (golden mouth) was given by his hearers, not by historians. Born in Antioch around 349, trained in classical rhetoric under the famous pagan teacher Libanius — who said on his deathbed that Chrysostom should have been his successor "if the Christians had not stolen him" — Chrysostom became a monk, ruined his stomach with desert austerities, returned to Antioch, was ordained a priest, and preached for twelve extraordinary years.
blocks.es_reference: Si recuerda solo a un predicador del cuarto siglo, recuerde a Crisóstomo. El apodo griego Chrysostomos (boca de oro) le fue dado por sus oyentes, no por los historiadores. Nacido en Antioquía alrededor del 349, entrenado en retórica clásica bajo el famoso maestro pagano Libanio — quien dijo en su lecho de muerte que Crisóstomo debería haber sido su sucesor «si los cristianos no me lo hubieran robado» — Crisóstomo se hizo monje, arruinó su estómago con austeridades del desierto, regresó a Antioquía, fue ordenado sacerdote, y predicó durante doce años extraordinarios.

blocks.en: His preaching method was expository: he preached straight through whole books of the Bible, sermon by sermon. We still possess hundreds of his homilies on Genesis, the Psalms, Matthew, John, Acts, and the entire Pauline corpus. He preached in plain Greek for ordinary people. He was unafraid to apply Scripture sharply to the moral life of his hearers, including the rich and the powerful. His most famous Antiochene sermons, the Statues homilies of 387, were preached during a tax revolt when citizens of Antioch had toppled imperial statues and feared the emperor's vengeance. Chrysostom preached daily through the crisis. The emperor pardoned the city.
blocks.es_reference: Su método de predicación era expositivo: predicaba directamente a través de libros enteros de la Biblia, sermón por sermón. Aún poseemos cientos de sus homilías sobre Génesis, los Salmos, Mateo, Juan, Hechos, y el corpus paulino entero. Predicaba en griego sencillo para gente común. No tenía miedo de aplicar la Escritura agudamente a la vida moral de sus oyentes, incluyendo a los ricos y poderosos. Sus sermones antioquenos más famosos, las homilías de las Estatuas del 387, fueron predicados durante una revuelta fiscal cuando los ciudadanos de Antioquía habían derribado las estatuas imperiales y temían la venganza del emperador. Crisóstomo predicó diariamente a través de la crisis. El emperador perdonó a la ciudad.

blocks.en: In 398 Chrysostom was effectively kidnapped from Antioch by imperial agents and consecrated bishop of Constantinople against his will. He immediately began reforming the clergy, attacking imperial luxury, and preaching against the morals of the court. The Empress Eudoxia became his enemy. He was exiled twice. He died on a forced march in 407, his last recorded words being, "Glory to God for everything." The man whose pulpit had once held the empire's capital died on a back road in obscurity. Three decades later his body was returned in honor to Constantinople. The pulpit had outlasted the throne.
blocks.es_reference: En 398 Crisóstomo fue efectivamente secuestrado de Antioquía por agentes imperiales y consagrado obispo de Constantinopla contra su voluntad. Inmediatamente comenzó a reformar el clero, a atacar el lujo imperial, y a predicar contra la moral de la corte. La Emperatriz Eudoxia se convirtió en su enemiga. Fue exiliado dos veces. Murió en una marcha forzada en 407, sus últimas palabras registradas siendo: «Gloria a Dios por todo». El hombre cuyo púlpito había sostenido una vez la capital del imperio murió en un camino trasero en oscuridad. Tres décadas después su cuerpo fue regresado en honor a Constantinopla. El púlpito había sobrevivido al trono.

blocks.en: Ambrose of Milan (c. 339–397)
blocks.es_reference: Ambrosio de Milán (c. 339–397)

blocks.en: In the West, the great preacher was Ambrose. A Roman governor and trained lawyer, he was acclaimed bishop of Milan by the people in 374 — while still unbaptized. Within a week he was baptized, ordained, and consecrated bishop. He spent the rest of his life trying to be worthy of an office he had never sought. When the Emperor Theodosius ordered the massacre of seven thousand citizens of Thessalonica in 390, Ambrose refused him communion until he did public penance. The emperor of the Roman Empire bowed to a bishop's pulpit. The picture is one of the great icons of fourth-century Christianity.
blocks.es_reference: En Occidente, el gran predicador fue Ambrosio. Un gobernador romano y abogado entrenado, fue aclamado obispo de Milán por el pueblo en 374 — mientras todavía no estaba bautizado. Dentro de una semana fue bautizado, ordenado, y consagrado obispo. Pasó el resto de su vida tratando de ser digno de un oficio que nunca había buscado. Cuando el Emperador Teodosio ordenó la masacre de siete mil ciudadanos de Tesalónica en 390, Ambrosio le rehusó la comunión hasta que hizo penitencia pública. El emperador del Imperio Romano se inclinó ante el púlpito de un obispo. La imagen es uno de los grandes íconos del cristianismo del cuarto siglo.

blocks.en: Ambrose's preaching also did one more thing of permanent consequence. A young North African professor of rhetoric named Augustine, drifting through Milan in 384 looking for something he could not name, went to hear Ambrose preach — at first only to study the famous bishop's technique. He stayed because the words began to find him. The conversion of Augustine, which we will meet in Unit 4, started in the pews of a sermon by Ambrose.
blocks.es_reference: La predicación de Ambrosio también hizo una cosa más de consecuencia permanente. Un joven profesor norteafricano de retórica llamado Agustín, vagando por Milán en 384 buscando algo que no podía nombrar, fue a oír a Ambrosio predicar — al principio solo para estudiar la técnica del famoso obispo. Se quedó porque las palabras comenzaron a encontrarlo. La conversión de Agustín, que conoceremos en la Unidad 4, comenzó en las bancas de un sermón de Ambrosio.

blocks.en: The Cappadocians as preachers, and Augustine's preaching manual
blocks.es_reference: Los Capadocios como predicadores, y el manual de predicación de Agustín

blocks.en: Basil's Hexaemeron (sermons on the six days of creation) is one of the great expository works of the early church. Gregory of Nazianzus's Five Theological Orations are sermons preached against the resurgent Arians, and they are among the most theologically dense sermons ever delivered. Gregory of Nyssa's homilies on the Beatitudes and the Lord's Prayer remain in print today as devotional reading. The fourth century closes (just barely — finished in 426) with the first Christian preaching manual ever written: Augustine's De Doctrina Christiana, Book IV. The Christian preacher, Augustine wrote, has the same three goals as the classical orator — to teach, to delight, and to move — but his materials are not invented; they are the inspired Scripture. The preacher's job is to make the text clear, attractive, and life-changing. Augustine's manual passed to the medieval church and through it to the Reformation, and the basic outline of his approach is still recognizable in any honest preaching course taught today. The fourth century did not invent preaching — the first century did. But the fourth century perfected it, refined it, gave it categories and manuals, and produced a body of expository work that has fed every great preaching age since.
blocks.es_reference: El Hexamerón de Basilio (sermones sobre los seis días de la creación) es una de las grandes obras expositivas de la iglesia primitiva. Los Cinco Discursos Teológicos de Gregorio de Nacianzo son sermones predicados contra los arrianos resurgentes, y están entre los sermones más teológicamente densos jamás entregados. Las homilías de Gregorio de Nisa sobre las Bienaventuranzas y el Padre Nuestro permanecen en imprenta hoy como lectura devocional. El cuarto siglo cierra (apenas — terminado en 426) con el primer manual de predicación cristiano jamás escrito: De Doctrina Christiana de Agustín, Libro IV. El predicador cristiano, escribió Agustín, tiene las mismas tres metas que el orador clásico — enseñar, deleitar, y conmover — pero sus materiales no son inventados; son la Escritura inspirada. El trabajo del predicador es hacer el texto claro, atractivo, y transformador de vidas. El manual de Agustín pasó a la iglesia medieval y a través de ella a la Reforma, y el bosquejo básico de su enfoque es aún reconocible en cualquier curso honesto de predicación enseñado hoy. El cuarto siglo no inventó la predicación — el primer siglo lo hizo. Pero el cuarto siglo la perfeccionó, la refinó, le dio categorías y manuales, y produjo un cuerpo de obra expositiva que ha alimentado cada gran era de predicación desde entonces.

blocks.en: Why This Matters for Ministry Today
blocks.es_reference: Por qué esto importa para el ministerio hoy

blocks.en: First, doctrine is not optional. Arius was not a bad man with bad theology. He was a popular preacher with a logical-sounding argument. The church survived him only because she had bishops who knew exactly which word, in which language, would hold the line.
blocks.es_reference: Primera, la doctrina no es opcional. Arrio no era un mal hombre con mala teología. Era un predicador popular con un argumento de sonido lógico. La iglesia lo sobrevivió solo porque tenía obispos que sabían exactamente qué palabra, en qué idioma, mantendría la línea.

blocks.en: Second, councils define what every pulpit must defend. When you preach Christ as fully God and fully man this Sunday, you are preaching Nicaea and Chalcedon. Honor the line. Stand on it.
blocks.es_reference: Segunda, los concilios definen lo que cada púlpito debe defender. Cuando predique a Cristo como plenamente Dios y plenamente hombre este domingo, está predicando Nicea y Calcedonia. Honre la línea. Párese en ella.

blocks.en: Third, the validity of the gospel does not depend on the worthiness of the preacher. The Donatist controversy taught the church a hard lesson: the sacrament is from Christ, not from the minister. This protects every congregation from the moral collapse of any pastor and every preacher from the unbearable weight of being the source of his own message.
blocks.es_reference: Tercera, la validez del evangelio no depende de la dignidad del predicador. La controversia donatista le enseñó a la iglesia una lección dura: el sacramento es de Cristo, no del ministro. Esto protege a cada congregación del colapso moral de cualquier pastor y a cada predicador del peso insoportable de ser la fuente de su propio mensaje.

blocks.en: Fourth, the second great century of preaching was the century of expository preaching through whole books. Chrysostom did not bounce from topical sermon to topical sermon. He preached through Genesis, then through Matthew, then through the Pauline corpus. Whole books. Verse by verse. Sunday by Sunday. The book-by-book pattern Chrysostom modeled has been the bedrock of every great preaching ministry since.
blocks.es_reference: Cuarta, el segundo gran siglo de la predicación fue el siglo de la predicación expositiva a través de libros enteros. Crisóstomo no rebotaba de sermón temático a sermón temático. Predicaba a través de Génesis, luego a través de Mateo, luego a través del corpus paulino. Libros enteros. Versículo por versículo. Domingo tras domingo. El patrón libro-por-libro que Crisóstomo modeló ha sido el cimiento de cada gran ministerio de predicación desde entonces.

blocks.en: Closing: The Empire Falls, the Church Endures
blocks.es_reference: Cierre: El imperio cae, la iglesia perdura

blocks.en: By 451, when the bishops adjourned at Chalcedon, the Roman Empire that had once been Christianity's persecutor and was now her patron was beginning to crumble. The western half would not survive the fifth century. In 410, Visigoths under Alaric sacked Rome itself for the first time in eight hundred years. The shock was so great that Augustine of Hippo would spend the last decade of his life writing The City of God to explain what had happened.
blocks.es_reference: Para 451, cuando los obispos se levantaron en Calcedonia, el Imperio Romano que una vez había sido perseguidor del cristianismo y ahora era su patrón comenzaba a desmoronarse. La mitad occidental no sobreviviría al quinto siglo. En 410, los visigodos bajo Alarico saquearon la propia Roma por primera vez en ochocientos años. El choque fue tan grande que Agustín de Hipona pasaría la última década de su vida escribiendo La Ciudad de Dios para explicar lo que había sucedido.

blocks.en: And the church would not die with the empire. The doctrines hammered out at Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon would carry the gospel intact through the centuries of barbarian darkness that came next. The expository preaching modeled by Chrysostom and Ambrose would become the heartbeat of monastic communities preserving the faith through the collapse. Pass this examination, and we will meet the most important figure of the next thousand years: Augustine of Hippo, the man who watched Rome fall and explained it in light of eternity. Unit 4 awaits.
blocks.es_reference: Y la iglesia no moriría con el imperio. Las doctrinas forjadas en Nicea, Constantinopla, Éfeso, y Calcedonia llevarían el evangelio intacto a través de los siglos de oscuridad bárbara que vinieron a continuación. La predicación expositiva modelada por Crisóstomo y Ambrosio se convertiría en el latido de las comunidades monásticas preservando la fe a través del colapso. Apruebe este examen, y conoceremos a la figura más importante de los próximos mil años: Agustín de Hipona, el hombre que vio caer a Roma y la explicó a la luz de la eternidad. La Unidad 4 espera.

mc.stem: What was the Edict of Milan, and why was it important?
options: It divided the Roman Empire into Eastern and Western halves
It officially separated Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy
It denied Christians the right to own Scriptures
It granted Christians freedom of worship in 313 and ended the era of imperial persecution
mc.why: The Edict of Milan (313), issued by Constantine and Licinius, granted freedom of worship and ended Roman persecution.

mc.stem: Who was the first Roman emperor to openly support Christianity?
mc.why: Constantine, after his vision and victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312, was the first emperor to openly support Christianity.

mc.stem: What was the Donatist controversy primarily about?
options: Whether sacraments administered by clergy who failed under persecution were valid
Whether Gentiles could be baptized without circumcision
Whether Easter should be on a fixed date
mc.why: Donatists held that sacraments by lapsed clergy (traditores) were invalid. The mainstream church taught the sacrament's validity depends on Christ, not the minister — ex opere operato.

mc.stem: What did Arius teach that triggered the most serious theological crisis of the fourth century?
options: That the physical world was created by an inferior deity
That Christ had only one nature
That the Son was a created being, not co-eternal with the Father — 'there was when He was not'
That Mary should not be called the mother of God
mc.why: Arius taught the Son had a beginning and was not co-eternal with the Father. Nicaea condemned this with the word homoousios.

mc.stem: What Greek word did Nicaea use to define the Son's relationship to the Father?
mc.why: Homoousios — 'of the same substance' — was Nicaea's central word. The Son is fully and equally God with the Father, not just similar (homoiousios).

mc.stem: In what year was the Council of Nicaea held?
mc.why: The First Ecumenical Council met at Nicaea in 325, called by Constantine, with about 318 bishops.

mc.stem: Who defended Nicene orthodoxy and was exiled five times by Arian or semi-Arian emperors?
mc.why: Athanasius — 'contra mundum' — defended Nicene faith for 45 years, was exiled five times to four countries, returned five times.

mc.stem: What did Athanasius give the church in his Easter letter of 367?
options: The first known list of the 27 NT books we still use today
mc.why: Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 listed the 27 NT books in the order we still use, formally closing the canon question.

mc.stem: Who were the three Cappadocian Fathers?
options: Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa
mc.why: Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus (the Theologian), and Gregory of Nyssa perfected the Trinity formula: one ousia in three hypostases.

mc.stem: What did the Council of Constantinople (381) accomplish?
options: It condemned Arius for the first time
It reaffirmed and expanded the Nicene Creed, especially on the Holy Spirit, finally crushing Arianism
mc.why: Constantinople (381) reaffirmed Nicaea, expanded the creed on the Holy Spirit, crushed Arianism. The Nicene Creed we recite today is the Constantinopolitan version.

mc.stem: What did the Council of Ephesus (431) decide?
options: That Christ has only one nature
That Mary is rightly called theotokos and condemned Nestorianism
That sacraments by lapsed clergy are valid
That the Son is of the same substance as the Father
mc.why: Ephesus condemned Nestorius and affirmed Mary as theotokos because the One she bore was truly God incarnate — one Person, fully divine and fully human.

mc.stem: What did the Council of Chalcedon (451) define about Jesus Christ?
options: One Person in two natures, fully God and fully man, united without confusion, change, division, or separation
mc.why: Chalcedon rejected both Nestorianism (two persons) and Monophysitism (one nature) and gave the church its definitive Christological formula.

mc.stem: Why is the fourth century considered one of the great centuries of Christian preaching?
options: Because the empire forced everyone to become Christian
Post-Constantine freedom, classical rhetoric meeting biblical content, doctrinal controversies forcing precision, urban congregations needing instruction, and the basilicas providing public spaces
Because preaching was no longer required to be biblical
mc.why: Five factors converged: freedom, education, controversy, audience, architecture. The result was a Golden Age that produced Chrysostom, Ambrose, the Cappadocians, and Augustine.

mc.stem: Who was nicknamed 'Golden Mouth' (Chrysostomos) by his hearers?
mc.why: John Chrysostom — born in Antioch, kidnapped to be bishop of Constantinople, exiled twice, died in 407 saying 'Glory to God for everything.'

mc.stem: What was distinctive about Chrysostom's preaching method?
options: He preached topical sermons on cultural issues
He preached expositorily, straight through whole books of the Bible, sermon by sermon
He read sermons word-for-word from prepared texts
He delivered only short homilies under five minutes
mc.why: Chrysostom's expository, book-by-book method left hundreds of homilies on Genesis, Psalms, Matthew, John, Acts, and the Pauline corpus — the bedrock pattern of every great preaching ministry since.

mc.stem: Which Western preacher's sermons were instrumental in the conversion of Augustine?
mc.why: Augustine went to Milan in 384 to study Ambrose's rhetorical technique. He stayed because the words began to find him. The conversion of Augustine started in the pews of a sermon by Ambrose.

mc.stem: What did Ambrose famously demand of the Emperor Theodosius after the Thessalonica massacre of 390?
options: That he go on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem
That he do public penance before being readmitted to communion
That he resign his army commission
mc.why: Ambrose refused Theodosius communion until he did public penance for the Thessalonica massacre. The emperor of Rome bowed to a bishop's pulpit — one of the great icons of fourth-century Christianity.

mc.stem: What is De Doctrina Christiana, Book IV?
options: The Latin translation of Athanasius's Easter letter
The first Christian preaching manual ever written
mc.why: Augustine's De Doctrina Christiana Book IV (finished 426) is the first Christian preaching manual. The preacher's three goals — to teach, delight, and move — but his materials are the inspired Scripture, not invention.

mc.stem: What is the formula by which the Cappadocians defined the Trinity?
mc.why: The Cappadocian formula — one ousia in three hypostases — has held the doctrine of the Trinity steady for sixteen centuries. One God in three Persons, equal in essence, distinct in person.

mc.stem: In what order did the four ecumenical councils of this period occur?
mc.why: The four great ecumenical councils of this era: Nicaea 325 (homoousios, anti-Arian), Constantinople 381 (Trinity completed), Ephesus 431 (theotokos, anti-Nestorian), Chalcedon 451 (one Person two natures).
